a48ee12e16:
The guide lists: tokens, context windows, sampling, non-determinism, next-token prediction; fast mode, extended thinking, adaptive thinking, effort levels; zero/single/multi-shot. That is worth two or three direct questions.

But these ideas also sit under most scenario stems in the exam. A cost question is a token question. A "flaky output" question is a sampling question. A latency question is an effort or fast-mode question.
663fa9b721:
A language model does one thing: given a sequence of tokens, it produces a probability distribution over the next token. Generation is a loop that picks one token from that distribution, appends it and asks again, so every cost, limit and latency is counted in tokens, and every output is a sample, not a lookup.

The knobs you control all act on that loop: sampling parameters on older models, thinking and effort on newer ones, fast mode on Opus, and the examples you put in the prompt. They change what the distribution is conditioned on, how a token is picked from it, and how many tokens the model spends before it answers.
330053ba35:
Predicting the next symbol is an old idea. In 1948 Claude Shannon estimated the entropy of English by asking people to guess the next letter of a text. He also built crude generators from letter and word frequency tables.

For the next fifty years, n-gram models did the same thing at scale. They counted how often each word follows the previous two or three words in a corpus, and turned the counts into probabilities. They powered speech recognition and phone keyboards. They also had the two weaknesses that shaped everything after them. They could not see further back than their n words. And they had no notion that "invoice" and "bill" mean similar things, so every rare phrase was a zero.
fa9236734d:
Neural language models (Bengio and colleagues, 2003) replaced the count table with a learned function that maps words to vectors, so similar words share statistical strength. Recurrent networks (RNNs, then LSTMs) carried a hidden state forward through the text and stretched the usable context to a few hundred words. But they processed one token at a time, during training as well as generation. That made them slow to train and forgetful over long spans.

The 2017 transformer ("Attention Is All You Need") removed the recurrence. Every position attends directly to every earlier position, and the whole training sequence is processed in parallel. That single change is why input tokens are cheap and fast today: the prompt is read in one parallel pass. Output tokens stay expensive and serial, because each new token still needs its own pass. Section 03 returns to that asymmetry, since it explains most latency questions.
bb8d2f4970:
Scaling did the rest. GPT-2 (2019) and GPT-3 (2020) showed that a large enough next-token predictor, given a few examples in its prompt, could perform tasks it was never explicitly trained for. The GPT-3 paper named that behaviour in-context learning. It also introduced the vocabulary of zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot that the exam guide still uses.

Raw pretrained models were hard to steer, though. They continued text rather than followed instructions. Instruction tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback (2022) turned them into assistants that answer the request. Anthropic's Constitutional AI work (2022) and the Claude models that followed belong to this stage.
e5cf43713d:
The latest stage is test-time compute: letting the model generate reasoning tokens before it answers, and training it to use them well. Prompting for "step by step" reasoning (chain of thought, 2022) showed the effect. Reasoning models made it a trained behaviour.

On the Claude API this arrived first as extended thinking with a fixed budget_tokens (Claude 3.7 Sonnet and the Claude 4 family). Then came adaptive thinking, steered by an effort level, where the model decides per request how much to think. Fast mode is a serving-side development of the same period: same weights, a faster inference configuration, a higher price.

So every item in objective 5.1 is a point on one line. There is a next-token predictor, the units it counts in, the window it sees, and the way a token is picked. Then there are the ways you buy more generation (thinking, effort) or faster generation (fast mode).
2a65464e72:
Generation wraps a loop around it. The model computes the distribution, the decoder picks one token, the token is appended to the sequence, and the model runs again on the longer sequence. It stops when it picks an end-of-turn token, when a stop sequence matches, when it emits a tool call, or when it reaches max_tokens.

Those exits are exactly the stop_reason values you handle in code (chapter 05): end_turn, stop_sequence, tool_use, max_tokens. There is also model_context_window_exceeded, for when the loop runs into the window.
89224eeb17: Output tokens are serial; input tokens are parallel. The model reads the whole prompt in one parallel pass (prefill), but it must run one step per output token. Three things follow. Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens. Time-to-first-token grows with prompt length, while total time grows mostly with output length. And the cheapest latency fix is usually asking for less output. A 4,000-token answer takes roughly ten times longer to generate than a 400-token answer on the same model.
7da2b91b10: Early tokens condition later ones. Once the model writes "The customer is eligible", every later token is predicted given that claim. A model that commits to an answer first and explains afterwards ends up justifying whatever it picked. That is why reasoning before answering helps on hard problems, whether through thinking or a "reason, then answer" format. The answer tokens are conditioned on the reasoning tokens, not the other way round.
119f019081:
Fluent is not the same as true. The training objective rewards plausible continuations. When the context does not contain the fact asked for, the most probable continuation is still a confident-sounding sentence. Hallucination isn't a malfunction of the mechanism. It is the mechanism working on missing evidence.

So the fixes are about the context: give the source, ask for quotes, allow "unknown". They are also about checking output (chapter 18). Telling the model to be accurate won't do it.
1b6ba0f1c6:
It helps to do one step with numbers. The companion's toy model (toy_lm.py, a bigram table with the same interface as a real model) is asked for the next token after your bill is. It returns one logit per vocabulary entry: due 2.2, paid 1.6, late 0.9, and -6.0 for the eight other tokens.

The softmax exponentiates each logit and divides by the sum. Here e2.2 = 9.03, e1.6 = 4.95, e0.9 = 2.46, and the eight others together contribute 0.02, for a total of 16.46. So P(due) = 9.03 / 16.46 = 0.548, P(paid) = 0.301, P(late) = 0.149, and every other token shares 0.001.

A real model does exactly this over a vocabulary of a hundred thousand or more tokens. Its logits come from a deep network instead of a table. The arithmetic of the last step is the same.
73f4f172e5:
Now loop. Suppose the draw picks due (55% of the time). The context becomes your bill is due, and the next distribution is today 0.505, now 0.306, . 0.186. Pick today, and then . follows with probability 0.999. The probability of the whole continuation due today . is the product: 0.548 × 0.505 × 0.999 = 0.277.

So even in a model with three plausible words per step, the single most likely three-token answer shows up in barely more than a quarter of runs. Real answers are hundreds of tokens long. That is why "the same request returns the same text" is the wrong expectation from the start (section 07). Companion 16_worked_sampling.py prints these numbers, so you can change the logits and watch them move.
5d1c650124:
A request has two phases with very different costs. Prefill reads the input. All prompt tokens are processed together in parallel, and the result is stored as a key/value cache so later steps do not recompute it. Decode generates the output: one forward pass per token, each reading the cache plus the tokens generated so far.

Time to first token (TTFT) is roughly queueing plus prefill, so it grows with prompt length. Prompt caching (chapter 15) cuts it, because a cached prefix skips most prefill work. Total time is TTFT plus output tokens divided by the output speed (output tokens per second, OTPS).

With illustrative numbers of 1.5 seconds TTFT and 50 OTPS, a 40-token reply finishes in 2.3 seconds. A 6,000-token report takes 121.5 seconds. Thinking tokens are output tokens, so they sit inside the decode phase, before any visible text.
f95caf5a2f:
This model is enough to answer most latency questions on the exam by elimination.

If the complaint is "nothing appears for a long time", look at TTFT: prompt size, caching, queueing, and hidden thinking before the first text. Streaming shows progress. display: "omitted" lets text start streaming sooner, because the server skips streaming the thinking text.

If the complaint is "it takes forever to finish", look at output tokens. Ask for less, lower effort, or raise OTPS with fast mode or a smaller model.

A design that only measures total latency cannot tell these apart. Log TTFT and output tokens separately.
d2be18b8c6:
Take a question the context cannot answer: "What is the early-termination fee on plan X-200?" with no tariff document attached. The model still has to produce a distribution over next tokens. And its training has seen many fee amounts in sentences shaped like this one.

Companion 24_why_hallucination.py sets illustrative logits for five continuations and shows the shape. With no source, the mass spreads over $150 (0.28), $200 (0.34), $250 (0.23) and $350 (0.14), with 0.01 on "not in the documents". So 76% of sampled answers are a confident wrong number, and each reads exactly as fluently as the true one.

Put the tariff excerpt in the context, and the true value takes 0.98 of the mass. Leave the source out but tell the model it may say the information is not in the documents, and that option takes 0.75. Confident wrong answers fall to 21%.
050be16029:
Three lessons come out of that toy, and they are the exam's lessons.

First, a hallucination is a sample from a spread-out distribution, not a bug in an otherwise exact process. You change the outcome by changing what the distribution is conditioned on (retrieval, tool results, quoted sources). Or you give the model a legitimate low-risk continuation: permission to abstain, an "unknown" enum value.

Second, the spread itself is a signal. High variation across repeated samples of the same factual question flags guessing. So does disagreement between a model's answer and its own quoted source.

Third, instructions like "be accurate" do little, because they do not add the missing evidence.
b5c6fb4600:
Format drift is the same mechanism acting on the first few tokens. Without a strong pattern, the first output token might be {, Sure, Here or The, each with real probability. Once Sure is drawn, the rest of the reply is conditioned on a chatty opening. The JSON, if it comes at all, ends up wrapped in prose.

On older models people fixed this by prefilling the assistant turn with {. On Claude 4.6 and later, a prefilled final assistant turn is a 400. Current options act earlier or harder. Structured outputs or a strict tool schema constrain the output at decode time. Examples (section 11) make the format the dominant continuation.

Long conversations add a slower drift. As instructions recede behind many turns, the most recent content dominates the conditioning. That is why chapter 16 repeats key constraints near the end of the context and keeps histories short.
5ad39142ae:
A token is a unit of text in the model's vocabulary. Often it's a word or part of a word; sometimes a single character or byte, sometimes a run of spaces.

The tokenizer is trained before the model, by a compression procedure (byte-pair encoding and its relatives). Start from bytes, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new vocabulary entry, and stop at a target vocabulary size. Frequent strings in the training data end up as single tokens. Rare strings fall apart into many small pieces.

You don't need the algorithm for the exam. You need its consequence: token count depends on how common the text's patterns were in the tokenizer's training data.
be466eb88d: Non-English text. Scripts such as Hindi, Thai, Japanese and Chinese use more UTF-8 bytes per character, and they were less frequent in tokenizer training. So the same sentence often costs two to three times the tokens of its English equivalent (exact ratios vary by tokenizer; measure). A multilingual support bot priced from English test data will be over budget in other markets.
19bb9ef02f:
Tokens matter in four places. Each one produces a different class of bug, so they are worth listing:

  • cost: input and output priced per million tokens, output higher (chapter 15);
  • limits: context window and max_tokens (section 05);
  • rate limits: input and output tokens per minute per organisation, separate from requests per minute (chapter 05);
  • latency: output tokens are generated one by one.
a06f0066d0:
There are two authoritative sources.

Before a call, use the token-counting endpoint (client.messages.count_tokens(...)). It takes the same model, system, messages and tools as a real request and returns input_tokens. It is free, rate limited separately from message creation, and counts under the tokenizer of the model you name. The docs call the result an estimate that can differ slightly from the billed count, so keep a small margin.

After a call, the usage object on the response is the billed truth: input_tokens, output_tokens, and the cache fields (cache_creation_input_tokens, cache_read_input_tokens).
04ac5938d9:
Companion 05_token_estimate.py shows how far chars/4 drifts for Hindi, Japanese, code and JSON, compared with a byte-aware estimate. 06_count_tokens_budget.py wraps count_tokens in a fit check with headroom.

In Java, the official SDK exposes the same endpoint (client.messages().countTokens(params); check the SDK docs for the exact builder names). The check belongs where any payload-size guard goes in a Spring service: before the outbound call, with a metric on the result.
decd8ba037:
Token questions on the exam are usually cost questions in disguise, so it pays to do one full accounting. Take a telecom support agent turn on the 5.5 models. The request carries a 1,200-token system prompt, six tool definitions totalling 1,500 tokens, 3,000 tokens of conversation history including tool results, and an 80-token new message.

Because tools are present, the API also adds its own tool-use system prompt. Per the tool-use pricing table, that's 286 tokens with tool_choice auto or none on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 (406 with any or tool on Haiku 5.5; 675 and 804 on Opus 4.7; 496 and 588 on Haiku 4.5). The model thinks for 900 tokens and answers in 250. Companion 17_cost_of_a_request.py does the arithmetic.
4ae8ac8386:
At the October 2026 list prices per million tokens (Opus 5.5 $4 input / $20 output, Sonnet 5.5 $2 / $10, Haiku 5.5 $0.10 / $0.50 for prompts up to 100k tokens), the call costs $0.0473 on Opus 5.5, $0.0236 on Sonnet 5.5 and $0.0012 on Haiku 5.5. Three things stand out.

First, output is only 16% of the tokens but about half of the cost on all three models, because output is priced at five times input. And 900 of those output tokens are thinking you may never see.

Second, the user's actual message is 1.3% of the input. Everything else is resent scaffolding and history.

Third, the 2,986-token stable prefix (system, tools, tool-use prompt) is exactly what prompt caching is for. Cached at the 5.5 models' cache-hit rate, it drops the Sonnet call to $0.0180, a 24% saving before any prompt is rewritten.

At a million calls a month, those differences are $23,632 versus $1,182 between Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. That's why model routing (chapter 15) and effort routing (section 09) are cost decisions first.
9e155fe817:
Images are tokens too, and their count is predictable. Per the vision docs, an image is cut into 28 × 28-pixel patches and costs ceil(width / 28) × ceil(height / 28) tokens after resizing. Models from Claude 4.7 on use a high-resolution tier (long edge up to 2,576 px, at most 4,784 tokens per image). Other models use the standard tier (1,568 px, at most 1,568 tokens).

A 1,000 × 1,000 product photo is 36 × 36 = 1,296 tokens on either tier. A 1,920 × 1,080 screenshot is where the tiers part. A standard-tier model resizes it to about 1,456 × 819 and charges 1,560 tokens. A high-resolution model doesn't resize it, and charges 69 × 39 = 2,691 tokens. A 4K screenshot is capped at 4,784.

So the same screenshot-heavy support flow can cost about 1.7 times more input after an upgrade from Haiku 4.5 to a 5.5 model, before prices are considered. Downscale on the client when you do not need the detail (companion 18_image_tokens.py reproduces the docs table).

PDFs are billed as text plus an image per page, so a 30-page scanned contract is tens of thousands of tokens. A request can carry at most 600 images or PDF pages on 1M-window models (100 on 200k models).
79511c3d9f:
The tokenizer change deserves its own arithmetic, because it catches teams who did everything else right. Per the token-counting docs, Claude 4.7 and later models produce approximately 30% more tokens for the same text; the exact increase depends on content. The 6,066-token request above would have measured about 4,666 tokens on an older model.

A capacity plan built on the old count is off by that same factor everywhere: input cost, output cost (the answer text is tokenized the same way), rate-limit usage and window fill. The fix is procedural. Recount representative prompts with count_tokens against the target model as part of the migration checklist. Then alert on usage per request class after the switch.
f3d805ae65: Java parallel: treat token counts like message size in a Kafka or JMS design. You would not size a topic from the average JSON payload measured on a different serializer. You measure on the real serializer, set max.request.size with headroom, and alert on outliers. Here count_tokens is the real serializer, the context window is the broker limit, and usage is the metric you put on a Micrometer counter tagged by model and request class.
020169ac3e:
The context window is the maximum number of tokens the model can attend to in one request: everything it reads plus everything it writes in that turn. Per the context-windows docs, it includes the system prompt, every message (tool results, images and documents included), tool definitions, cached and uncached input alike, and the output generated in the turn, including thinking tokens.

The model has no memory outside it. The API is stateless, so a conversation only "remembers" what you resend (chapter 05).
c854c3ed0a:
Sizes, as of October 2026 per the docs: the newest models have a 1M-token window by default, with up to 128k output tokens per request. Those are Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.6 to 4.8, and Sonnet 4.6. Other models, including Haiku 4.5, have 200k.

Long-context requests are billed at standard rates on the 1M models. The exception is Haiku 5.5, where prompts over 100,000 tokens cost more (check chapter 15 and the pricing page).
b67e658889:
Two overflow behaviours are worth memorising.

If the input alone exceeds the window, every model returns a 400 invalid_request_error ("prompt is too long").

If the input fits but input plus max_tokens does not, it depends on the model. Claude 4.5 and later models accept the request. If generation actually reaches the limit, they stop with stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded". Earlier models reject the request up front.

So on current models, a large max_tokens is no longer a reason for a 400. But a long agent run can end mid-answer with a stop reason your loop must handle.
f5eb92767c:
Thinking adds two details.

First, thinking tokens come out of max_tokens. A 16,000 cap with 14,000 tokens of thinking leaves 2,000 for the answer, and a max_tokens stop with nothing but a thinking block is a real outcome.

Second, previous turns' thinking blocks are treated differently by model. On Opus 4.5 and later Opus models, Sonnet 4.6 and later Sonnet models, and Haiku 5.5, the API keeps them by default and they count as input. On earlier models and Haiku 4.5, the API strips them automatically. Either way, within a tool-use exchange you must send the thinking block back unmodified with its tool results (chapter 05 covers the wire format).
cfb9e7dd28: A bigger window is capacity, not quality. Models retrieve facts less reliably from the middle of very long contexts than from the start and end. And every token you add is paid for on every call that resends it. "It fits in 1M tokens" is not a design. Chapter 16 covers keeping the window lean with pruning, compaction, retrieval and subagents.
b58efdeb1e: The window is easy to state and easy to overfill. Several contributors are invisible in the code that builds a request. The table lists everything that counts, per the context-windows and token-counting docs, along with the trap each one sets.
7cf3a030cd:
Retention of earlier thinking is the newest of these, and the one most likely to surprise. On models that keep thinking blocks, each turn's reasoning is resent and counted as input on every later call. It is billed as output once when generated, then as input when resent.

Companion 25_context_budget.py runs a five-turn agent conversation: a 2,000-token system prompt, 4,000 tokens of tools, tool results between 3,000 and 25,000 tokens, two screenshots (1,560 and 2,691 tokens) and between 800 and 3,000 tokens of thinking per turn. By turn five the input is 74,107 tokens when thinking is kept and 66,307 when it is stripped. That's 7,800 extra tokens on every subsequent call, from reasoning nobody reads. Context editing (thinking block clearing) or compaction can remove them when that matters (chapter 16).
12d447da4b:
Two smaller mechanics complete the picture.

Context awareness: per the docs, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5 receive their token budget in the system prompt. They also get a usage update after each tool call (a <system_warning> such as "Token usage: 35000/200000; 165000 remaining"), so they can pace long tasks. Opus 4.7 and later, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 don't get this; the docs point to task budgets (beta) instead.

Long outputs and HTTP: per the thinking docs, the SDK requires streaming when max_tokens exceeds 21,333. For more than about 32k thinking tokens per request, the docs recommend the Batch API to avoid timeouts. A 128k max_tokens on a non-streaming call is a client-side error before it is a window question.
4a341e452a:
The model gives a distribution, and something must pick one token from it.

Greedy decoding always takes the most probable token. It sounds safest, but it tends to produce repetitive, flat text and can lock into loops. The most probable next token after a repeated phrase is often the phrase again.

Sampling draws a token at random in proportion to its probability. That gives natural variety, and it is the default. Three parameters reshape the distribution before the draw:
fe1057e78b: The usual folk advice was "temperature 0 for analytical tasks, higher for creative ones". The docs historically suggested adjusting temperature or top_p, not both. Two facts make that advice weaker than it sounds. First, low temperature reduces variation but does not make outputs identical (section 07). Second, and more important for the exam, the newest models do not accept the parameters at all.
bdc855510f:
Per the thinking docs as of October 2026, some models reject any non-default temperature, top_p or top_k with a 400 on every request, whether or not thinking is on. They are Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.8, Opus 4.7 and the Fable and Mythos models.

There are two sharp edges. On those models the default top_p is 0.99, so top_p: 1 is itself a 400. And a request that sends both temperature and top_p fails even at their defaults.

On older models (for example Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5) the parameters work. The exception is manual extended thinking: with it on, temperature and top_k are incompatible, and top_p must be between 0.95 and 1.
8a0a786a97: Model 4.6 row: the 4.6 restriction follows the "older models" rule in the docs; check the docs for your exact model. The design lesson does not depend on the row. Consistency on current models comes from the prompt, examples, structured outputs and validation, not from sampling knobs. A shared config that sets temperature: 0 for every call becomes a production outage the day someone changes the model ID.
0b5fc64b17: Companions 02 to 04 let you watch the mechanism on a numpy toy model. Temperature changes the spread but never the ranking. top_p keeps one token when the model is confident and three when it is not. And 10,000 draws reproduce the probabilities. 08_sampling_param_guard.py turns the table above into a request validator.
40d2fc542e:
Read the table as mechanisms.

Dividing by T = 0.5 doubles every gap between logits (2.2 versus 1.6 becomes 4.4 versus 3.2). So the top token grows from 0.548 to 0.727, but paid still appears in about one run in five. Low temperature narrows the distribution; it does not remove it.

Raising T to 1.5 gives the junk tail sixteen times more mass (0.0012 to 0.016). That's where incoherent tokens come from at high temperature.

top_k = 2 and top_p = 0.8 give the same result here only by coincidence. On a confident step where due had 0.95, top_p 0.8 would keep one token while top_k 2 would still keep two. That adaptivity is why nucleus sampling became the common default in open models.
e26154c4c0:
Two consequences matter for design.

First, per-token probabilities multiply. If each of 200 output tokens has a 0.99 chance of matching the "usual" choice, the chance that a whole reply matches is 0.99200 = 0.13. Exact-match expectations on free text are hopeless even at modest randomness. What you can stabilise is the decision the text expresses: a label, a field, a yes or no.

Second, on Claude's newest models none of these knobs is available. The table models what the serving stack does at its defaults; it is not a menu. The exam uses this material to test two things: whether you know what temperature does (spread, not ranking; less variation, not none), and whether you know not to reach for it.
3c160cd20b: Send the same request twice and you may get two different answers. Some people treat this as a defect to switch off. It is better treated as a property of the component, like network latency, that the design must absorb. There are four sources, and only the first is under the caller's control at all:
708e0c8225: Sampling. With default settings each token is a random draw. A token with 15% probability appears in roughly 15% of runs. Once it appears, every later token is conditioned on it, so one early divergence can produce a completely different answer.
db5ff520a3: Numerical non-determinism in serving. Large-scale inference batches requests together and runs floating-point arithmetic in parallel. The order of additions can differ between runs, which changes logits in the last decimal places. When two tokens are nearly tied, that is enough to flip the choice. This is why even greedy decoding on older models was not guaranteed to be reproducible.
5c24ef3527:
The goal is not identical bytes. It is a system whose outcomes are acceptable on every run. The useful question for any feature: if this call returned a different, still-plausible answer, what would break? The answer sorts features into three groups:

  • Free-text features (summaries, explanations, drafts) tolerate variation. They need quality evaluation, not exact matching.
  • Structured decisions (classification, extraction, routing) need the output space constrained and validated.
  • Side-effecting actions (refunds, plan changes, emails) need idempotency and approval, because a retried or varied call must not act twice or act wrongly.
1baacce0cf: Constrain the output space. Structured outputs or a strict tool schema remove whole classes of variation (field names, JSON syntax, label spelling). An enum of labels with an explicit "unclear" value gives the model a legitimate place to put ambiguity, instead of guessing differently each time (chapter 18).
d08c9ce096: Validate and retry with the error. A deterministic validator decides whether the reply is usable. On failure, one or two repair attempts that include the exact validation error usually succeed. After that, dead-letter or route to a human (chapter 12).
ee0afcd90f: Companion 09_nondeterminism_harness.py runs three telecom tickets 50 times each against a fake that samples from a fixed distribution. The clear tickets agree over 90% of the time. The ambiguous one ("upgrade fee on my bill after outage") does not, and that is the case to fix in the prompt. 10_design_for_nondeterminism.py combines validation, bounded retry, majority vote and an idempotency key.
f58b66e9d0: Options that propose temperature: 0 to make output deterministic are wrong twice on current models. The parameter is rejected with a 400. And even where it is accepted, it does not guarantee identical output. Prefer the option that constrains and validates the output, measures stability over repeated runs, or caches an approved answer.
30902436b4:
Once variation is accepted, the eval question becomes statistical. If a case fails with probability f on each run, n independent runs show at least one failure with probability 1 − (1 − f)n.

Companion 19_how_many_runs.py tabulates it. A case that fails 10% of the time is seen in a single run only 10% of the time. Five runs catch it 41% of the time, ten runs 65%, and it takes 29 runs to see it with 95% confidence. A 5% failure needs 59 runs; a 1% failure needs 299.

That is why "we ran it and it passed" is not evidence of stability. It is also why stability evals target the classes that matter rather than every case.
57249c614c: The same reasoning applies to a pass rate. Nine passes out of ten looks like 90%, but the 95% Wilson interval runs from 60% to 98%. At 45 of 50 it narrows to 79% to 96%; at 180 of 200, to 85% to 93%. So when two prompt versions score 88% and 91% on 50 cases, you have not shown that either is better. Size the eval so the interval is narrower than the difference you need to detect, and compare versions on the same cases.
eafbc6fa3a:
Two metrics from agent evaluation make the trade-off explicit. pass@k is the chance that at least one of k attempts succeeds. It is useful when a verifier can pick the good one, such as code that must pass tests. pass^k is the chance that all k succeed, which is what a customer experiences over k conversations.

With a per-run success rate of 0.9, pass@3 is 0.999, while pass^3 is 0.729. A demo shows pass@k; production lives on pass^k. Reliability work moves the per-run rate, because pass^k punishes every point of it.
ae72f2e1c4:
Between "exact text" (always flaky) and "no test" (always blind) sits the tolerant assertion: check the properties that must hold on every acceptable reply. For a billing reply those are:

  • a parseable structure with the right keys;
  • a label from the allowed set;
  • required facts present (the month, the amount);
  • numbers within tolerance (12.5 and "12.50" are the same refund);
  • forbidden content absent (a card number pattern).

Companion 20_tolerant_assertions.py runs a fake that returns three differently worded correct replies 95% of the time, and two kinds of bad reply otherwise. All three wordings pass, both bad shapes fail, and the eval reports a 95% pass rate over 40 samples. The exact-text assertion would have passed about one run in three, and caught neither bad reply for the right reason.
cc94889ccf:
For judgements that resist rules (is the summary faithful, is the tone acceptable), the same structure holds with a model-graded check. That is a separate grader call with a rubric and a constrained verdict, calibrated against human labels on a sample (chapter 12 and the CCAR-P evaluation chapters).

In JUnit the shape is identical. Use AssertJ's isCloseTo(12.5, within(0.01)), isIn(LABELS) and doesNotContainPattern on a parsed record, inside a parameterised test that runs N samples and asserts a pass-rate threshold. Tag it so it runs in a nightly eval job rather than the unit build.
29e1c2622b:
Section 03 explained why reasoning before answering helps: answer tokens conditioned on worked reasoning are more likely to be right on multi-step problems. Extended thinking makes that a feature. The model generates thinking blocks (its reasoning) before the text or tool calls of its answer.

Thinking tokens are output tokens. They are billed as output, count against max_tokens, the context window and output rate limits, and add latency. Thinking helps most on multi-step reasoning, maths, code, planning, and agent turns that must decide what to do with a tool result. It adds little to simple lookups, formatting or chit-chat.
4fdd573db3: Manual (extended) thinking: thinking: {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N}. You set a token budget for reasoning, and it must be below max_tokens (minimum 1,024; check the docs for the budget rules). This is the only mode on Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5 and earlier. It is deprecated on Opus and Sonnet 4.6, and a 400 on the newest models.
8d88800341: Adaptive thinking: thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}. There is no budget. The model decides per request whether to think and how much, steered by the effort level (section 09). It interleaves thinking between tool calls automatically, with no beta header. It is the only thinking mode on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Opus 4.7 and 4.8, and a 400 on 4.5 and earlier models.
c58f31c7e6: You pay for what you cannot see. On the newest models the default display is "omitted". The thinking block arrives with an empty thinking field and an opaque signature, but the tokens are billed. "summarized" returns a summary (no charge for producing the summary) and is the default on 4.6 and earlier. Never estimate cost from visible text; read usage.
d808d92d2c: Restrictions. No assistant prefill (on 4.6 and later it is a 400 regardless of thinking). Manual thinking allows only tool_choice auto or none. Adaptive allows forced tool use, except on Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Fable/Mythos 5.1, which reject forced tool use on every request. Changing thinking settings between turns invalidates prompt-cache breakpoints (chapter 15).
58faf38ca0:
On models that still take {"type": "enabled", "budget_tokens": N} (Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, and deprecated on the 4.6 models), the extended-thinking docs set the rules:

  • the minimum budget is 1,024 tokens;
  • it must be less than max_tokens, except with interleaved thinking, where the budget spans all thinking blocks in one assistant turn and may exceed max_tokens;
  • it is "a target rather than a strict cap", so the model may stop well short.

The docs suggest starting near the minimum for simple tasks and at 16,000 or more for complex ones, then raising it step by step. Use the Batch API for budgets above 32k, because very long requests hit timeouts. Changing budget_tokens between requests invalidates message-level cache breakpoints, so pick one per cached conversation.
3892e26396:
Thinking buys accuracy on problems where an intermediate step can be wrong: arithmetic over several figures, plans with dependencies, code that must satisfy constraints, deciding what a tool result implies. It buys nothing where the answer is a lookup or a reformatting. The cost is in output tokens, and therefore in decode time.

Take the docs' own example, a GCD question on an Opus model: 312 thinking tokens and 36 answer tokens, 348 billed. At an illustrative 50 output tokens per second, the visible 36-token answer would take under a second on its own. With thinking it takes about seven, and with display: "omitted" the user sees nothing during the first six. At Opus 5.5's $20 per million output tokens, that answer costs $0.0070 instead of $0.0007.

For a GCD that is waste. For a billing dispute where the alternative is an agent hour, it is cheap.
dc7bb9d3e1:
Adaptive thinking changes the economics in tool loops. Per the adaptive-thinking docs, the first request after new user input usually carries most of the reasoning. Follow-up requests that only process tool results can skip thinking, and thinking per request tends to fall as the conversation grows.

No request is guaranteed a thinking block at any effort level, so code must not assume content[0] is thinking. Interleaved thinking (reasoning between tool calls) is automatic and needs no beta header. The trace below is the typical shape of a three-call agent turn.
8fb2b827fd: Display has a latency side as well as a visibility side. Per the thinking docs, display: "omitted" reduces latency, not cost. The server skips streaming the thinking text, so the answer starts streaming sooner. "summarized" streams a summary of the reasoning at the same billed cost. That is useful for a UI that shows progress, or for an audit log. A beta "updates" display (header thinking-display-updates-2026-08-18) streams progress updates instead; check the docs before using it.
b4c2e5c376:
Effort is the control that replaced the thinking budget as the main cost and quality dial. You set it as output_config: {"effort": ...}, a top-level request field separate from thinking. It has five values: low, medium, high, xhigh, max.

The docs describe it as "a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget". It tells the model how much work to put into the whole response: how often and how deeply it thinks, how long its text is, and how many tool calls it makes.
52221a1026: Effort works with or without thinking. It also affects tool behaviour, which is easy to miss. At lower effort the model tends to combine operations into fewer tool calls, act without preamble and confirm tersely. At higher effort it makes more tool calls, explains its plan and writes fuller summaries. So for an agent that bills per tool call or hits rate-limited backends, effort is a load control as well as a quality control. Setting effort to the model's default is identical to omitting it.
a7743d04df:
Two model-specific interactions with thinking come from the effort docs. Haiku 5.5 and Opus 5 allow thinking: {"type": "disabled"} only at high effort or below. Sonnet 5.5's "between_tools" mode is a 400 at xhigh and max.

A newer beta lets a mid-conversation role: "system" message change effort per turn (beta header mid-conversation-output-config-2026-07-01; check the docs before relying on it). Don't pass "adaptive" as an effort value. Adaptive is a thinking mode, not a level.
0c1ad60e1a:
How to choose: start from the model default, build an eval for the feature, and try one level lower. If quality holds, keep the cheaper level. If it drops, try one level higher and check whether the gain is worth the tokens.

Route by task class rather than setting one effort for the whole application. A support bot can run greetings and FAQ answers at low, account changes at the default, and complex dispute investigation at high. This is the same idea as model routing (chapter 15) at a finer grain. It is usually tried first, because it does not change the model's behaviour profile or price list.
1b6c01dec2: The effort docs give a starting recommendation per model, and they differ enough to be worth a table. The advice is the same each time: start where the docs say, then run an effort sweep on your own eval. Don't carry settings over from an earlier model, because levels are recalibrated between releases. The docs say this explicitly for Sonnet 5.5 relative to Sonnet 5, and note that lower levels on Fable 5 often exceed xhigh on prior models.
f1eb0caec9:
Effort applies to all output tokens: thinking, text, tool calls and their arguments. The docs add that max_tokens is the hard limit, while effort is soft guidance. So a cost ceiling must be set with max_tokens (and handled as a stop reason), not with effort alone. For xhigh or max on Opus 4.7, 4.8 and 5, the docs suggest starting at 64k max_tokens; for agentic coding on Sonnet 5.5, 128,000 with streaming.

Changing top-level effort between requests restarts the prompt cache. The per-message beta (a role: "system" message with empty content and output_config.effort) preserves it on the models that support it: Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, Opus 5.5, Opus 5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5.
f076a7f23e: Companion 21_effort_sweep.py runs the method on a synthetic model shaped like the docs describe, for two task classes and 400 cases per level. The rule it applies is statistical rather than "highest score wins". It picks the lowest level whose 95% interval reaches the best level's lower bound, because a one-point gain inside the noise is not worth doubling the tokens.
c3e17b0473: The numbers are synthetic, but the shape is the real decision. FAQ answers gain nothing measurable above low, and they pay four to thirteen times the tokens for it. Disputes gain nineteen points from low to high. The last two points, up to xhigh, cost 84% more tokens and 37 more seconds. Whether that is worth it is a product decision, and the sweep makes it explicit. Run the same sweep again after every model change.
64d7c6a63f: Constraints: switching speed invalidates the prompt cache, since fast and standard do not share cached prefixes. It is not available in the Batch API or with Priority Tier. It has a separate rate limit, with 429 and a retry-after header when exceeded. Access is by waitlist or account manager.
d81e6a5dd5: The arithmetic follows from the prefill/decode model in section 03. Fast mode multiplies output tokens per second by up to 2.5 and leaves time to first token alone. On Opus 5.5 it doubles the per-token price ($8 / $40 against $4 / $20). Companion 22_fast_mode_fallback.py uses an illustrative 1.5-second TTFT, 50 OTPS standard and the full 2.5x speed-up, with an 8,000-token prompt:
a2ace133bb:
The price doubles in every row; the benefit only becomes large when output is long. Input is also billed at the fast rate across the whole context. So a long prompt with a short answer is the worst case: double the input bill for a fraction of a second. And because switching speed invalidates the prompt cache, mixing fast and standard calls within one cached conversation pays cache writes twice.

Fast mode has its own rate limit (headers anthropic-fast-input-tokens-* and anthropic-fast-output-tokens-*). When it is exceeded, the API returns 429 with retry-after. The SDK retries 429s twice by default, and since fast mode replenishes continuously, the wait is usually short.
f34c64b29d: The docs describe an opt-in fallback for when waiting is worse than paying the cache miss. Send the fast request with max_retries=0, catch the rate-limit error, and resend without speed. But max_retries=0 also disables the SDK's retries for overloaded and server errors, so the fallback must handle those itself.
5f64370d2f:
Keep them apart.

  • Thinking mode decides whether the model reasons in thinking blocks.
  • Effort decides how much work it puts into the whole response, thinking included. It changes quality, tokens and cost.
  • Fast mode changes how quickly the same tokens are produced on Opus, at a higher price, with no quality change.

A stem that wants "same quality, faster long outputs, cost acceptable" points to fast mode. "Cheaper and faster on easy requests" points to lower effort or a smaller model.
6a07932dca:
A "shot" is a worked example in the prompt: an input and the output you want for it. Zero-shot gives only the instruction. One-shot adds one example. Few-shot (the guide says multi-shot) adds several, typically two to five.

No weights change. The examples work through the mechanism of section 03. Once the context contains several input/output pairs in a consistent format, the most probable continuation of a new input is an output in that same format: the same fields, length, tone and labelling conventions. This is called in-context learning.
24ad5b0b20:
Three rules make shots work, and they are what scenario questions test.

Vary the examples so the only thing they share is what you want copied: different lengths, different labels, and at least one hard or borderline case. Examples of easy cases teach little.

Keep them consistent with the instructions. When the examples and the text disagree, the model often follows the examples.

Mark them clearly, for example inside <example> tags in the system prompt. Then the model won't treat them as part of the current conversation or the current customer's data.

Chapter 17 covers writing and maintaining examples in detail. The CCAR-F guide's few-shot chapter covers using them to calibrate extraction and review tasks.
57d3e0e9d9:
Few-shot examples are input tokens on every call. Eight examples of 60 tokens each add about 500 tokens per request. At 200,000 requests a day, that is 100 million tokens a day.

Put them in the stable prefix of the prompt and cache them (chapter 15). Then check with an eval whether fewer examples, or structured outputs alone, give the same result. On current models a schema often fixes format with zero examples, and the examples are then spent on judgement calls instead.
af7f33b868: Shots and thinking combine. With thinking on, examples still steer output format. Examples that show reasoning in the expected style can also steer how the model reasons. On adaptive models, though, it is usually better to state what to consider and let the model think. If you previously used a "think step by step" one-shot to get chain-of-thought, adaptive thinking replaces that.
ff9442c7e6:
Companion 23_shots_measured.py turns the claims above into numbers. It classifies 40 telecom tickets five times each under four prompts. There are 32 clear tickets and 8 borderline ones, such as "Upgrade fee appeared after the outage", where house policy says anything about money is billing. The model is a fake that simulates in-context behaviour:

  • without examples, its format drifts;
  • with one example, it copies the example's format and often its urgency value;
  • with several varied examples, one of which shows the borderline rule, it follows both format and rule;
  • a fourth arm uses three near-identical billing examples.

It is a simulation, so the exact figures are not evidence about Claude. The directions match what the docs and practice report, and the harness is the template for running the same comparison on a live model.
ac20656659:
Each row teaches one rule.

Zero-shot fails mostly on format, not on understanding. On a real model you would add structured outputs before examples, and its label accuracy would rise to match.

One example fixes format immediately but leaks its particulars: 72% of answers copy its "high" urgency, against a true base rate near a third.

Three examples that are all alike are worse than one. The only regularity they show is "billing, high", and labels drift towards it.

Varied examples that include the borderline rule are the only arm that gets the hard cases right. They cost about four times the zero-shot input tokens: $16 per million calls at Haiku 5.5 prices, and $660 at Opus 5.5 prices. That cost is why examples belong in the cached prefix. It is also why the experiment to run on your own data is "how few varied examples hold the borderline accuracy".
1c6a45f4e2:
Multishot and caching fit together naturally on the Claude API. Examples are stable text, so they sit in the system prompt before the cache breakpoint. On the 5.5 models a cache hit costs 0.05 times the base input price.

Keep examples free of real customer data, because they are sent on every call and logged with every request. Put them inside <example> tags so the model can tell them from the live input. And version them like code: changing an example changes behaviour on every input that resembles it.
8076f6aee4:
None of this chapter is Python-specific, and a Spring service is where many of these rules end up enforced. Four patterns cover most of it.

The official Java SDK (com.anthropic:anthropic-java) builds requests with MessageCreateParams.builder(). If your SDK version has no typed setter for a newer request field, send it with putAdditionalBodyProperty. Check the SDK docs for the exact builder names for output_config, thinking and count_tokens in your version. The shapes below follow the JSON the docs define.
6bee9f991f: 1. Effort and model routing as configuration, validated at startup. The routing table from section 09 is configuration, not code. A bad value should stop the application from starting, rather than fail on the first customer request. Bad values include an unknown level, xhigh on a model that lacks it, or "adaptive" passed as an effort.
12905523f3: 2. Token budgets like payload limits. A TokenBudgetGuard bean calls the count-tokens endpoint for requests above a size threshold. The endpoint is free but rate limited, so skip it for small requests. The guard rejects requests that would not fit with headroom, and records usage from every response on Micrometer counters tagged by model and route. That is the same structure as a size check on an outbound SOAP or Kafka payload. It turns a tokenizer change after a migration into a dashboard shift instead of an invoice surprise.
5621acae3e: 3. Stop reasons as an exhaustive switch. Java 21 pattern matching over the stop reason turns the "handle every loop exit" rule from section 05 into a compile-time habit. Treat max_tokens and model_context_window_exceeded as a typed TruncatedResponseException the caller must handle. Default unknown values to an error, not to "return the text".
066f237079:
4. Tests that respect non-determinism. Unit tests use a stub client: WireMock serving recorded JSON, or a fake implementation of your own LlmClient interface. That keeps them deterministic, and they run in the normal build. Stability and quality checks are a separate JUnit 5 suite tagged @Tag("eval"). It runs nightly against the live API, using tolerant assertions over N samples.

Mixing the two (live calls with exact asserts in the unit build) is the Java version of the broken test in section 07. It produces the same flaky pipeline.
81e0c7b12d:
Run bash run_all.sh in ccdvf-companion/13-llm-fundamentals/. Then work through these, in order:

  • change the temperature in 02 and confirm the ranking never changes;
  • set top_p to 0.5 in 03 and see the nucleus collapse to one token;
  • add a Spanish and a Korean sample to 05 and compare estimates;
  • in 09, change the ambiguous ticket's distribution to 0.8/0.2 and see how many runs you need before the harness flags it;
  • in 11, add Haiku 5.5 with thinking disabled at xhigh and make the builder refuse it.

Then the new examples:

  • change the logits in 16 and recompute the table by hand before running it;
  • in 17, move the six tools to Haiku 5.5 with tool_choice: any (406 overhead tokens) and see the share change;
  • in 19, find how many runs a 2% failure needs;
  • in 21, cut N to 50 and watch the picked level become unstable;
  • in 23, delete the borderline example from the varied arm and see which column falls.

If you have an API key, run 06_count_tokens_budget.py --live on your own prompts and compare against usage after a real call.
6beb3298ae:
Done when you can:

  • explain why the same request gives different answers;
  • list the four places tokens matter;
  • say which models reject temperature;
  • write an adaptive-thinking request with an effort level from memory;
  • compute the softmax for three logits by hand;
  • say how many runs a 10% flaky case needs;
  • cost a request part by part, including the tool-use system prompt and an image;
  • say when fast mode is and is not the right latency fix.
